questions.stem: A 63 year old postmenopausal woman sees her GP with 5 months of aching bones, constipation and vague abdominal pain. She has felt low and passed a renal stone 2 years ago. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Raised calcium with a raised PTH and low phosphate is primary hyperparathyroidism; all PTH-independent causes (myeloma, sarcoid) suppress PTH.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.

clues: aching bones, constipation and vague abdominal pain
steps.x: **Stones, bones, abdominal groans, psychiatric overtones** in a postmenopausal woman, with raised calcium AND raised PTH.

elim: FHH is asymptomatic and lifelong; she has stones, bones and groans.
Myeloma hypercalcaemia suppresses PTH; her PTH is raised.
Sarcoid raises calcium via vitamin D with suppressed PTH.
Secondary disease has a low or normal calcium, not a raised one.

steps.x: **C. Primary hyperparathyroidism.** High calcium + high PTH = primary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man has an adjusted calcium of 2.92 mmol/L (2.20–2.60) and a PTH of 12.8 pmol/L (1.6–8.5) on routine bloods. His renal function is normal. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. He has lost some skin turgor and his mucous membranes are dry.
questions.q: Which symptom is he most likely to report?
questions.e: Hypercalcaemia causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, so polyuria, thirst and dehydration are typical. Tetany and tingling belong to hypocalcaemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Raised calcium driven by PTH, and he is **dehydrated**: high calcium stops the kidney concentrating urine.

elim: Spasm and tetany are features of hypocalcaemia.
Heat intolerance points to hyperthyroidism.
Paraesthesia around the mouth is a hypocalcaemia symptom.
Hypercalcaemia does not cause weight gain.

steps.x: **D. Polyuria and polydipsia.** High calcium = polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, fatigue.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman is found to have an adjusted calcium of 2.74 mmol/L (2.20–2.60) on bloods taken for a medication review. A repeat sample confirms it, with a PTH of 9.6 pmol/L (1.6–8.5) and phosphate of 0.72 mmol/L (0.80–1.50). She has no symptoms and no family history of calcium problems.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Most primary hyperparathyroidism is a single parathyroid adenoma; hyperplasia and carcinoma are less common, and PTH-independent causes suppress PTH.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
PTH-driven hypercalcaemia with low phosphate, sporadic and asymptomatic: **primary hyperparathyroidism**.

elim: Metastatic hypercalcaemia suppresses PTH.
Hyperplasia is less common and suggests MEN1 or a family history.
Carcinoma is a rare cause, usually with very high calcium.
Excess vitamin D suppresses PTH.

steps.x: **D. Solitary parathyroid adenoma.** Commonest cause of primary hyperparathyroidism: a single adenoma.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease from diabetic nephropathy attends renal clinic with aching bones. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Low calcium, high phosphate, low vitamin D and a raised PTH in CKD is a compensatory (secondary) rise in PTH. Tertiary disease needs a raised calcium.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
CKD means phosphate retention and poor vitamin D activation, so calcium falls and PTH rises **appropriately**.

elim: PTH would be low, not three times the upper limit.
Osteoporosis has a normal bone profile.
Primary disease raises calcium and lowers phosphate.
Tertiary disease has a raised calcium; his is low.

steps.x: **D. Secondary hyperparathyroidism.** Low calcium + high PTH in CKD = secondary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman had a renal transplant 14 months ago after 11 years of haemodialysis. Her graft function is good. She now has thirst, constipation and bone pain. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Years of secondary stimulation leave the glands secreting PTH autonomously, so calcium stays high even once the kidney is fixed: tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Long-standing CKD, now **hypercalcaemia with a very high PTH** even after the cause was corrected.

elim: Malignancy suppresses PTH; hers is very high.
Milk-alkali syndrome suppresses PTH and needs high calcium intake.
Secondary disease has a low or normal calcium.
Graft function is good and rejection does not cause this bone profile.

steps.x: **D. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism.** High PTH + high calcium after long CKD = tertiary.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman has amenorrhoea and milky nipple discharge for 6 months. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Investigations: prolactin 2850 mU/L (<500), adjusted calcium 2.79 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), PTH 10.9 pmol/L (1.6–8.5). Her brother had a pancreatic tumour removed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.e: Parathyroid, pituitary (prolactinoma) and pancreatic tumours are the three Ps of MEN1. MEN2A also has hyperparathyroidism but with thyroid and adrenal tumours.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
**Pituitary** (prolactinoma), **parathyroid** (raised calcium and PTH) and a family **pancreatic** tumour.

elim: MEN2A pairs hyperparathyroidism with medullary thyroid cancer and phaeochromocytoma, not pituitary tumours.
MEN2B has medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma and a marfanoid habitus.
NF1 causes neurofibromas and café-au-lait spots.
VHL causes haemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma.

steps.x: **A. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.** Parathyroid + pituitary + pancreas = MEN1.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man with MEN1 and hyperparathyroidism has 4 months of burning epigastric pain, reflux and watery diarrhoea despite a full course of omeprazole. Endoscopy shows multiple ulcers in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. Helicobacter pylori testing is negative.

visual.title: Where the pain is
visual.caption: Epigastric pain from multiple refractory peptic ulcers.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his ulcers?
questions.e: Multiple refractory ulcers beyond the duodenum with diarrhoea in MEN1 is Zollinger-Ellison syndrome from a pancreatic or duodenal gastrinoma.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.

clues: despite a full course of omeprazole
steps.x: Refractory ulcers in unusual places with diarrhoea in **MEN1**: acid hypersecretion from gastrin.

elim: Glucagonoma causes diabetes and necrolytic migratory erythema.
Insulinoma causes fasting hypoglycaemia.
No NSAID history, and jejunal ulcers suggest acid hypersecretion.
VIPoma causes profuse watery diarrhoea and hypokalaemia but not ulcers.

steps.x: **A. Gastrinoma.** MEN1 + refractory ulcers + diarrhoea = gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison).

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has had three episodes of renal colic in 4 years. Stone analysis shows calcium oxalate. He drinks 2 litres of fluid a day and takes no medicines. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.77 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 0.70 mmol/L (0.80–1.50), urate normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his stones?
questions.e: Recurrent calcium stones with hypercalcaemia and low phosphate point to primary hyperparathyroidism; check PTH.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Recurrent **calcium** stones plus **high calcium, low phosphate**.

elim: Cystinuria forms cystine stones and calcium is normal.
Gout gives urate stones; his urate is normal.
His fluid intake is adequate and does not explain hypercalcaemia.
Hyperoxaluria raises urinary oxalate but does not cause hypercalcaemia.

steps.x: **E. Primary hyperparathyroidism.** Recurrent calcium stones + hypercalcaemia: think primary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman in a care home has become withdrawn, lethargic and intermittently confused over 6 weeks. She is drinking more and is constipated. Urine dipstick is negative. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Investigations: sodium 141 mmol/L (135–145), TSH normal, adjusted calcium 3.08 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), PTH 14.2 pmol/L (1.6–8.5).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her confusion?
o: Delirium due to urinary tract infection
questions.e: Hypercalcaemia causes psychiatric overtones (depression, lethargy, confusion); the raised PTH makes primary hyperparathyroidism the cause.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Confusion, low mood, thirst and constipation with **calcium over 3** and a raised PTH.

elim: Dementia does not cause thirst, constipation or hypercalcaemia.
She is afebrile and the dipstick is negative.
Her sodium is normal.
Her TSH is normal.

steps.x: **C. Hypercalcaemia due to primary hyperparathyroidism.** Psychiatric overtones are a hypercalcaemia feature: always check calcium in new confusion.

questions.stem: A 56 year old woman has 1 day of severe epigastric pain radiating to her back with vomiting. She drinks no alcohol and abdominal ultrasound shows no gallstones. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Investigations: amylase 1620 U/L (<100), triglycerides normal, adjusted calcium 2.94 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), PTH 13.1 pmol/L (1.6–8.5).

visual.title: Where the pain is
visual.caption: Epigastric pain radiating to the back: acute pancreatitis.

questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of her pancreatitis?
questions.e: Hypercalcaemia is a recognised cause of pancreatitis (abdominal groans); a raised PTH makes primary hyperparathyroidism the cause once gallstones and alcohol are excluded.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Pancreatitis without gallstones or alcohol, and calcium is **high** (pancreatitis itself usually lowers it).

elim: She does not drink.
Ultrasound shows no gallstones.
Her triglycerides are normal.
She has not had an ERCP.

steps.x: **E. Primary hyperparathyroidism.** Unexplained pancreatitis + high calcium + high PTH = hyperparathyroidism.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with primary hyperparathyroidism has found it hard to climb stairs and rise from a low chair for 3 months. She has aching in her shins and ribs. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Bone tenderness with proximal muscle weakness
Carpopedal spasm on BP cuff inflation
Distal sensory loss in a glove-and-stocking pattern
Facial twitching on tapping the cheek
questions.e: High PTH and calcium cause bone tenderness and proximal weakness. Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs are hypocalcaemia signs, the classic confusion.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.

clues: climb stairs and rise from a low chair
aching in her shins and ribs
steps.x: Trouble with stairs and chairs is **proximal** weakness; aching bones means bone tenderness.

elim: Trousseau's sign is a sign of hypocalcaemia.
That is a peripheral neuropathy, not a feature of high PTH.
Chvostek's sign is a sign of hypocalcaemia.
Upper motor neurone signs point to cord pathology.

steps.x: **A. Bone tenderness with proximal muscle weakness.** Hyperparathyroidism on examination: bone tenderness and proximal weakness.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman fractured her wrist falling from standing. A DEXA scan shows a T-score of −2.9 at the distal radius. She takes no steroids and is not hyperthyroid. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.78 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 0.68 mmol/L (0.80–1.50), PTH 11.0 pmol/L (1.6–8.5), ALP 164 U/L (30–130).
questions.q: Which is the most likely secondary cause of her osteoporosis?
questions.e: PTH-driven bone resorption causes osteoporosis and fragility fractures, typically at cortical sites like the distal radius; raised calcium with raised PTH confirms the cause.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Fragility fracture and osteoporosis with **high calcium, low phosphate and high PTH**.

elim: Coeliac disease causes low or normal calcium.
She takes no steroids, and Cushing's does not raise calcium and PTH.
Osteomalacia has a low calcium and phosphate with raised PTH.
She is not hyperthyroid, and PTH would be suppressed.

steps.x: **D. Primary hyperparathyroidism.** Check a bone profile in osteoporosis: hyperparathyroidism is a treatable cause.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with polyuria, constipation and aching bones has a raised adjusted calcium and a raised PTH. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg. Renal function and vitamin D are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the rest of her bone profile?
o: Normal phosphate and very high ALP only
questions.e: PTH makes the kidney waste phosphate, so phosphate falls; increased bone turnover raises ALP when bone is involved.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.

clues: raised adjusted calcium and a raised PTH
Renal function and vitamin D are normal
steps.x: Primary disease with **bone symptoms** and normal kidneys.

elim: This pattern fits hypoparathyroidism.
High phosphate fits CKD-related secondary disease, not primary.
Bone involvement raises ALP, it does not lower it.
That fits Paget's disease, with normal calcium.

steps.x: **D. Low phosphate and raised ALP.** Primary hyperparathyroidism: high calcium, high PTH, low phosphate, high ALP if bone involved.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has 2 months of fatigue, thirst and constipation. Her GP finds an adjusted calcium of 2.83 mmol/L (2.20–2.60). Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Examination is normal. The GP wants to confirm the cause of the hypercalcaemia.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Repeat bone profile with serum PTH
questions.e: Hyperparathyroidism is a biochemical diagnosis: calcium with a PTH. Localisation scans come later and only once the biochemistry confirms it.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
Hypercalcaemia with no cause yet: PTH splits PTH-driven from PTH-independent causes.

elim: Imaging for malignancy comes only if PTH is suppressed.
DEXA assesses complications, not the cause.
Sestamibi localises an adenoma only after biochemical confirmation.
Neck imaging localises an adenoma only after the diagnosis is made biochemically.

steps.x: **C. Repeat bone profile with serum PTH.** Diagnose biochemically (bone profile + PTH) before any scan.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man has primary hyperparathyroidism confirmed on two bone profiles with PTH. He has had a renal stone and is listed for surgery. An ultrasound of the neck shows no parathyroid lesion. His pulse rate is 68 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg. The surgeon wants to localise the gland before operating.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: CT of the neck without contrast
Fine needle aspiration of the thyroid
questions.e: Sestamibi is taken up avidly by parathyroid adenomas and is used after biochemical confirmation, especially when ultrasound is normal.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
Diagnosis already confirmed; ultrasound **normal**; surgeon needs a location.

elim: Non-contrast CT is poor at finding small parathyroid adenomas.
FNA samples thyroid nodules and is avoided in parathyroid lesions.
The biochemistry is already confirmed twice.
This assesses thyroid function, not parathyroid adenomas.

steps.x: **D. Technetium-99m sestamibi scan.** Localise with sestamibi after biochemistry, especially if ultrasound is normal.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman has newly confirmed primary hyperparathyroidism with an adjusted calcium of 2.72 mmol/L (2.20–2.60). She has no symptoms. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. Her endocrinologist wants to know whether there is end-organ damage to bone before deciding on surgery.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Osteoporosis is a key end-organ complication and an indication for surgery; DEXA measures bone density.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
Asymptomatic disease: the decision rests on **complications** like osteoporosis.

elim: Marrow biopsy is for myeloma or marrow infiltration.
An isotope bone scan looks for metastases or Paget's.
Plain films are insensitive for reduced bone density.
This screens for myeloma, not bone density.

steps.x: **B. DEXA scan.** Assess bone with DEXA; also renal function and urinary calcium.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has an adjusted calcium of 2.68 mmol/L (2.20–2.60) and a PTH of 8.9 pmol/L (1.6–8.5). He has no symptoms. His mother and sister have been told they have 'slightly high calcium' that never needed treatment. His pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Urinary calcium separates primary hyperparathyroidism (normal or high) from familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (very low), which needs no surgery.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
Mild, asymptomatic, **familial** hypercalcaemia with a borderline PTH: could be FHH.

elim: PTHrP is for malignancy, which suppresses PTH.
ACE is for sarcoidosis, which suppresses PTH.
Myeloma suppresses PTH.
Localisation is premature until FHH is excluded.

steps.x: **E. Urinary calcium.** Check urinary calcium before surgery to exclude FHH.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has aching legs and tiredness. She works night shifts and rarely goes outside. Her renal function is normal. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.14 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 0.78 mmol/L (0.80–1.50), PTH 13.6 pmol/L (1.6–8.5), ALP 182 U/L (30–130).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to establish the cause?
questions.e: Low calcium with a raised PTH and normal kidneys is secondary hyperparathyroidism, most often from vitamin D deficiency; her lack of sunlight fits.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
**Low** calcium with **high** PTH and healthy kidneys, little sunlight.

elim: Low magnesium lowers PTH; hers is raised.
Her calcium is low, so this is not an adenoma.
Thyroid disease does not cause this bone profile.
Her renal function is normal.

steps.x: **A. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D.** Secondary hyperparathyroidism with normal renal function: check vitamin D.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with hypertension takes bendroflumethiazide. She has mild thirst. Bloods show an adjusted calcium of 2.76 mmol/L (2.20–2.60) and PTH of 10.2 pmol/L (1.6–8.5). Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 142/86 mmHg. She is not confused or vomiting.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Stop bendroflumethiazide and encourage oral fluids
questions.e: First-line care is hydration and stopping drugs that raise calcium (thiazides, lithium); then definitive management can be planned.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Mild symptomatic hypercalcaemia on a **thiazide**, which reduces urinary calcium loss.

elim: Loop diuretics are not first-line and worsen dehydration.
Mild, stable hypercalcaemia does not need admission.
Restricting calcium raises PTH further and is not advised.
Cinacalcet is for those unfit for surgery, not the first step.

steps.x: **E. Stop bendroflumethiazide and encourage oral fluids.** Hydrate and stop thiazides or lithium first.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man's GP receives a result showing an adjusted calcium of 3.52 mmol/L (2.20–2.60). On the phone his wife says he has been vomiting for 2 days, is very sleepy and muddled and is barely drinking. He has known primary hyperparathyroidism and is on a surgical waiting list.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Bring forward his outpatient surgical appointment
Oral rehydration at home and repeat bloods in 1 week
questions.e: Calcium over 3.5 with vomiting, dehydration and confusion is a hypercalcaemic crisis needing urgent hospital IV fluids and specialist care.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Severe hypercalcaemia with **dehydration, vomiting and confusion**: a crisis.

elim: Surgery is not the emergency step.
He cannot drink and is confused; this is unsafe.
Too slow for a crisis.
Diet change does nothing for a hypercalcaemic crisis.

steps.x: **C. Same-day hospital admission.** Hypercalcaemic crisis = urgent admission.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with primary hyperparathyroidism is admitted with confusion and vomiting. Her adjusted calcium was 3.61 mmol/L (2.20–2.60). She has had 4 litres of IV 0.9% sodium chloride over 24 hours and now passes good volumes of urine. Repeat calcium is 3.22 mmol/L. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: After rehydration, an IV bisphosphonate is given if calcium remains high in a hypercalcaemic crisis; it stops osteoclast bone resorption.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.

clues: now passes good volumes of urine
steps.x: Fully rehydrated, still **above 3**: needs something to stop bone resorption.

elim: Calcium would make hypercalcaemia worse.
Steroids help vitamin D-driven causes like sarcoid, not PTH-driven disease.
Oral bisphosphonates act too slowly in a crisis.
Thiazides raise calcium further.

steps.x: **C. IV zoledronic acid.** Crisis: IV saline first, then an IV bisphosphonate if calcium stays high.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has primary hyperparathyroidism with an adjusted calcium of 2.95 mmol/L (2.20–2.60). He has had two renal stones and a DEXA scan shows osteopenia. Sestamibi shows a single right inferior adenoma. He is otherwise well with a pulse rate of 70 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism in a fit patient is cured by parathyroidectomy; cinacalcet is for those unfit for surgery.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Fit, symptomatic (stones, bones), with a **localised adenoma**.

elim: Cinacalcet is reserved for patients unfit for surgery.
Fluids treat symptoms but not the cause.
Treats bone density but not the adenoma.
Radioiodine treats the thyroid, not the parathyroids.

steps.x: **D. Parathyroidectomy.** Definitive treatment of primary hyperparathyroidism: surgery.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man had a renal transplant 2 years ago after a decade on dialysis. His graft works well. He has persistent hypercalcaemia with bone pain. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.86 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), PTH 52.0 pmol/L (1.6–8.5), creatinine 124 µmol/L (60–110). His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
questions.e: Tertiary hyperparathyroidism is autonomous gland secretion and is definitively treated with parathyroidectomy.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Long CKD, now high calcium and very high PTH despite a working kidney: **tertiary** disease.

elim: Activated vitamin D would worsen his hypercalcaemia.
Calcium supplements worsen hypercalcaemia.
His graft works; dialysis does not fix autonomous glands.
A phosphate binder treats secondary disease with high phosphate.

steps.x: **C. Parathyroidectomy.** Tertiary hyperparathyroidism: parathyroidectomy.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman of South Asian heritage has aching bones and fatigue. Her renal function is normal. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.18 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), PTH 12.4 pmol/L (1.6–8.5), 25-OH vitamin D 16 nmol/L (>50). Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency is treated by replacing vitamin D; PTH falls once calcium normalises.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Low calcium, high PTH, **very low vitamin D**, normal kidneys.

elim: Lowering PTH would worsen her low calcium.
IV fluids treat hypercalcaemia; hers is low.
Her glands are responding appropriately; surgery is not indicated.
There is no adenoma to find in secondary disease.

steps.x: **B. Colecalciferol replacement.** Secondary hyperparathyroidism: treat the cause (vitamin D).

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease, not yet on dialysis, has a raised PTH. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.12 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 2.02 mmol/L (0.80–1.50), PTH 31.0 pmol/L (1.6–8.5). His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg. The renal team plans the first step.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Dietary phosphate restriction and a phosphate binder
questions.e: In CKD, phosphate retention drives secondary hyperparathyroidism, so phosphate, calcium and vitamin D are managed together by renal teams, starting with phosphate control.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
CKD with **high phosphate** and low calcium driving PTH.

elim: Thiazides are ineffective at this eGFR and do not treat PTH.
Bisphosphonates treat hypercalcaemia; his calcium is low.
Surgery is for tertiary disease, not first-line secondary disease.
High phosphate drives PTH and must be treated.

steps.x: **B. Dietary phosphate restriction and a phosphate binder.** CKD secondary hyperparathyroidism: control phosphate, calcium and vitamin D with renal input.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has newly diagnosed primary hyperparathyroidism with an adjusted calcium of 2.79 mmol/L (2.20–2.60). She is thirsty, passes urine often and feels tired. She is alert and eating normally. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. She awaits a surgical opinion.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Mild symptomatic hypercalcaemia is managed with hydration while definitive surgery is arranged; IV fluids are for severe disease.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Mild hypercalcaemia, alert and drinking: **hydration** while awaiting surgery.

elim: She is alert, eating and only mildly hypercalcaemic.
Calcium would worsen hypercalcaemia.
Thiazides raise calcium.
Vitamin D can raise calcium further in primary disease.

steps.x: **C. Increase oral fluid intake.** Mild hypercalcaemia: oral hydration first.

questions.stem: An 88 year old woman with severe aortic stenosis has symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism. She is judged unfit for parathyroidectomy and is started on cinacalcet. Her adjusted calcium falls from 2.98 to 2.64 mmol/L over 2 months.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of cinacalcet?
o: Allosteric activation of the calcium-sensing receptor
Blockade of PTH receptors on osteoblasts
Inhibition of osteoclast farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase
questions.e: Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic: it makes the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor more sensitive, so the gland 'sees' more calcium and releases less PTH.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
A drug used when surgery is not possible, which **mimics calcium** at the gland.

elim: Cinacalcet acts on the parathyroid gland, not the PTH receptor.
That is how bisphosphonates work.
Cinacalcet does not act on vitamin D activation.
That is denosumab.

steps.x: **A. Allosteric activation of the calcium-sensing receptor.** Cinacalcet = calcimimetic at the calcium-sensing receptor.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman with primary hyperparathyroidism has bone pain and an ALP of 188 U/L (30–130). Histology of a bone biopsy shows increased numbers of osteoclasts. A student asks how PTH increases osteoclast activity when osteoclasts have no PTH receptors.
questions.q: Which cell does PTH act on directly to increase bone resorption?
questions.e: PTH binds osteoblasts, which express RANKL and so activate osteoclasts to resorb bone and release calcium.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Osteoclasts are activated **indirectly**: something else must carry the signal via RANKL.

elim: Chondrocytes make cartilage, not bone signalling.
Macrophages are not the PTH target in bone.
Osteoclasts lack PTH receptors and are stimulated indirectly.
Chief cells secrete PTH; they are not its target in bone.

steps.x: **C. Osteoblasts.** PTH → osteoblasts → RANKL → osteoclasts.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with a parathyroid adenoma has an adjusted calcium of 2.84 mmol/L (2.20–2.60) and PTH of 12.0 pmol/L (1.6–8.5). Measurement shows a raised 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. His dietary calcium intake is normal but gut calcium absorption is increased.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for his raised 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D?
o: Increased skin synthesis of vitamin D
Reduced renal 24-hydroxylase breakdown from low phosphate alone
questions.e: PTH stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, raising active vitamin D, which increases gut calcium absorption.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
